title: A raffle drum with three dials
allegory: Sampling is a raffle: every word holds tickets in proportion to its probability and you draw one, while temperature reprints the tickets, top-k keeps only the biggest holders in the drum, and top-p keeps the biggest holders until they cover a set share of all tickets.
map: reprinting the tickets with the temperature dial
dividing logits by T: low T sharpens, high T flattens, the ranking never changes
only the k biggest holders stay in the drum
top-k: keep the k largest logits, set the rest to -inf
keep the biggest holders until they cover p of the tickets
top-p: the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches p, cut inclusively
drawing one ticket from the drum
sampling one token from the renormalised distribution
where_else: The temperature, top_k and top_p parameters of every text-generation API
Beam search, which keeps several partial sentences instead of drawing one token at a time
Sampling actions from a softmax policy in RL, where temperature trades exploring against exploiting
Evals that sample the same prompt many times at T > 0 to measure how often a behaviour appears

hamming.what: The step that turns the model's next-token probabilities into one actual token, with temperature, top-k and top-p as the knobs.
hamming.when: Every time a language model writes text, one token at a time.
hamming.why: Likelihood is a good training objective but a bad decoding objective: always taking the top token gives bland, repetitive text, so how you draw shapes what the same model says.

object.title: The raffle drum
object.subtitle: Eight candidate words, three rows: the model's odds, after the temperature dial, and after the cut.

cap.1: Eight candidate words and the tickets each holds. The front row is the model's own odds; the rows behind show what the dials do.
cap.2: Row 1: softmax(logits). Row 2: after temperature. Row 3: after top-k and top-p, renormalised. The logits are illustrative.
cap.3: Order as in ARENA's sample_next_token: frequency penalty, then temperature, then truncation, then one draw.

cap.1: Turn the temperature down: the favourite grabs almost all the tickets. Near zero this becomes 'always pick the top word'.
cap.2: Dividing logits by T below 1 sharpens the distribution; T → 0 is greedy argmax decoding.
cap.3: softmax(z/T) tends to one-hot on the argmax as T → 0 and to uniform as T → ∞; the ranking never changes.

cap.1: Turn it up: the tickets spread out and long-shot words get a real chance. Livelier text, and riskier.
cap.2: T above 1 flattens the distribution, so low-probability tokens are drawn more often.
cap.3: Higher T raises entropy. Because the argsort is unchanged, T alone never changes which tokens are eligible.

cap.1: Top-k: only the three biggest holders stay in the drum, and their tickets are topped up to fill it.
cap.2: top_k=3 keeps the three largest logits and renormalises over them.
cap.3: A fixed count ignores the distribution's shape: too many survivors when it is peaked, too few when it is flat.

cap.1: Top-p: keep the biggest holders until they cover 90% of the tickets. Here that keeps five words.
cap.2: top_p=0.9 keeps the smallest prefix whose running total reaches 0.9, including the one that crosses it.
cap.3: The inclusive cutoff guarantees kept mass ≥ p and a non-empty set; the survivors are then renormalised.

cap.1: Same 90% rule, colder temperature: now only two words survive. The two dials work together, not separately.
cap.2: Lowering T reshapes the running total, so the nucleus shrinks. Top-p and temperature interact.
cap.3: T rescales probabilities before the cumsum, so it changes the nucleus size; with top-k it only reweights a fixed set.

predict.q: You lower the temperature from 1 to 0.5. Can a different set of words survive top-k?

options.t: No, temperature never changes the ranking
Yes, low temperature reorders the words

predict.why: Dividing logits by T keeps their order, so the top-k set is identical; only the shares inside it change.

predict.q: Top-p with p = 0.1, and the top word alone holds 0.3 of the probability. How many words survive?
predict.why: Keep up to and including the first word that takes the running total past p, so the set is never empty.

predict.q: Why not always pick the single most likely word?

options.t: It tends to produce bland, repetitive text

predict.why: Holtzman et al. (ICLR 2020): likelihood is a good training objective but a bad decoding objective.

object.where: Anywhere a distribution has to become one decision: text generation, RL actions, evals that sample many times.
